title: AI's latest casualty? The health of the people building it.
excerpt: Lilian Weng of Thinking Machines Lab is the only the latest tech executive to resign due to stress and illness.
content_html:
Forget the environment or job opportunities. AI's latest casualty might be the health of the people building it.

Thinking Machines Lab cofounder Lilian Weng said she's stepping down from her role because of stress and illness. Weng, who also spent time at OpenAI, didn't disclose a specific diagnosis but said she's been ill more often in the past seven months than at any other point in her life.

"I don't feel I'm able to continue at the pace a startup requires," Weng wrote in a note to colleagues.

She's not alone, as evidenced by the internet's response to her exit. The pressures of the highly competitive AI race are taking a toll on the people involved in it.

Earlier this year, OpenAI executive Fidji Simo took medical leave before stepping away completely from her full-time role to become a part-time advisor. Simo, who was also an executive at Meta and Instacart's CEO, suffers from postural tachycardia syndrome, or POTS. The chronic illness causes heart palpitations, lightheadedness, and fainting.

XAI cofounder Greg Yang also shifted into an informal advisory role after he was diagnosed with Lyme disease. Yang said he'd sometimes sleep 12 hours a day but still couldn't recover, adding that he needed to "go founder mode on my health."

Could this be the start of a kinder, gentler era for tech employees?

The tech industry has spent the past few years touting the need to go "hardcore" and enter "founder mode" to compete. In theory, tech executives burning out from such a hectic pace should lead to a rethink of the entire strategy.

In theory, that is.

The reality is the AI race stops for no one. There are trillions of dollars at stake, and a general sense that any slowdown risks losing your competitive edge.

It's also notable that the executives stepping away are often one level removed from the big boss. The CEOs, meanwhile, remain firmly in place.

One of the few recent health-related departures involving a big boss — C3.ai's Tom Siebel — is also pretty telling. Siebel, who resigned in 2025 because of autoimmune disease-related vision problems, returned to the helm in May, telling CNBC the company's performance was "candidly unacceptable."

In the meantime, maybe read about how top leaders manage burnout.

Just be sure to get back to work quickly.

Dan DeFrancesco

content_html_zh:
忘记环境或工作机会。 人工智能的最新受害者可能是构建它的人的健康。

Thinking Machines Lab 联合创始人 Lilian Weng 表示，由于压力和疾病，她将辞去职务。 翁也曾在 OpenAI 工作过，她没有透露具体的诊断结果，但表示她在过去七个月里生病的次数比她一生中任何时候都多。

“我觉得我无法继续按照初创公司所需的速度发展，”翁在给同事的一份报告中写道。

她并不孤单，互联网对她退出的反应就证明了这一点。 竞争激烈的人工智能竞赛所带来的压力正在给参与其中的人们带来损失。

今年早些时候，OpenAI 高管 Fidji Simo 先请了病假，然后完全辞去全职职务，成为一名兼职顾问。 Simo 还曾担任 Meta 和 Instacart 的首席执行官，他患有姿势性心动过速综合症（POTS）。 这种慢性疾病会导致心悸、头晕和昏厥。

XAI 联合创始人 Greg Yang 在被诊断患有莱姆病后也转任非正式顾问。 杨说，他有时每天睡 12 个小时，但仍然无法恢复，并补充说他需要“进入健康的创始人模式”。

对于科技员工来说，这会是一个更友善、更温和的时代的开始吗？

过去几年，科技行业一直在宣扬需要“硬核”并进入“创始人模式”来竞争。 从理论上讲，科技高管因如此忙碌的节奏而精疲力竭，应该会导致对整个战略的重新思考。

理论上是这样。

现实是人工智能竞赛没有人会停下来。 这涉及数万亿美元，而且人们普遍认为任何经济放缓都有可能失去竞争优势。

还值得注意的是，离职的高管往往与大老板相差一级。 与此同时，首席执行官们仍然坚守岗位。

最近为数不多的涉及大老板的健康相关离职之一——C3.ai 的汤姆·西贝尔（Tom Siebel）——也很能说明问题。 西贝尔因自身免疫性疾病相关的视力问题于 2025 年辞职，并于 5 月重新掌舵，他告诉 CNBC，该公司的业绩“坦率地说是不可接受的”。

与此同时，也许可以了解高层领导者如何管理倦怠。

请务必尽快恢复工作。
